lines.note: Continues toricaye from the preceding page: exchanging garments, offices, or hostages. The new Item introduces lending below; the scan shows doubled f in officios.
Adds lending money, rice, and similar goods. The relative clause que continues into the terms of repayment on the next row.

runs.text: pagão em couſas da meſma eſpecie, & nu-

lines.note: The borrowed goods are repaid in things of the same kind and number. The clear c in eſpecie corrects OCR eſperie; nu- begins numero below.
Mero completes numero, followed by the printed example caualo. The text is preserved even though a horse is a less obvious example than money or rice; it does not authorize rewriting the gloss.
Torikaeshi is taking something back or recovering it. Re- begins recolher across the physical line break.
Completes recolher a cousa: recover or gather back the thing. This short continuation belongs to toricayexi.
Torichigae means taking one thing for another. The Portuguese por governs outra on the next row.

runs.text: outra. ¶ Item, Tomar entre ſi. i,

lines.note: Completes the mistaken-identification sense, then adds reciprocal taking or exchange. Tori- begins the explanatory Japanese synonym toricauasu below.
Completes torikawasu and begins the example sakazuki wo torichigayuru, exchanging drinking cups. Vt is italic; the Japanese example remains upright.

runs.text: Tomar, & dar entre ſi o Sacazzuqui.

lines.note: Ru completes the verb; the translation describes taking and giving the sake cup to one another. Sacazzuqui is a Japanese object name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, printed in the surrounding italic here.
Torichirashi is scattering things while handling them. The capital T is consistent with the visible headword and replaces OCR F.
The gloss continues: scatter something and leave it in disorder. The close printed joining in deixalaſem is retained rather than silently regularized.
Toriko denotes a captive or someone taken in war. The Portuguese catiuo gives the noun sense directly.
Toriko ni suru is making someone a captive. The Portuguese infinitives tomar and catiuar are completed by the wartime setting below.
Specifies capture in war, completing the preceding example. This physical line is part of the torico entry.
Torikobochi means dismantling or demolishing. Deſ- begins desmanchar, whose following explanation concerns buildings taken apart for rebuilding or timber recovery.

runs.text: manchar como caſas, &c. pera ſe tornarem a

lines.note: Completes desmanchar and specifies buildings dismantled so that they can be erected again. The final a belongs to tornarem a edificar below.

runs.text: edificar, ou ſe guardar a madeira.

lines.note: Finishes the two purposes of dismantling: rebuilding or preserving the timber. Madeira is the reusable construction material.
Torikome means enclosing or surrounding someone. The punctuation after cercar is a comma, not the OCR s; meo retains the historical spelling of the middle.

runs.text: a alguem de maneira que não fuja.

lines.note: The enclosure prevents a person from escaping. This purpose clause completes the definition of toricome.

Torikoroshi is killing through possession by a devil or kami. In Portuguese the postposed o diabo, ou Cami supplies the agent of matar; it is not an instruction to kill a deity. The printed capital Ca- continues below.
Mi completes Cami, and entrando em alguem describes the possessing being entering a person. This explains the agent and mechanism of the preceding matar gloss.
Torikube means putting firewood into a fire. The direct Portuguese gloss supports the Japanese verb meaning to feed or stoke it.
Torikui means taking something and eating it. The initial T of Tomando belongs to the same italic gloss as the rest, and the carons over u are retained.

Completes the eating gloss, then gives musato torikuu with the alternative torikurau. The example describes eating without selection; the printed final form and lack of a visible final full stop are retained.

runs.text: Comer qual quer couſa ſem eſcolha, ou com

lines.note: The Japanese example is translated as eating anything without choosing. The separate qual quer is the printed spacing, not modern qualquer.
Completes com desordem, adding disorderly or indiscriminate eating. This short row closes the toricui entry.
Torikumi here means grappling with someone by the hands. The headword begins with the visible T, correcting OCR F; al- continues into alguem.
Completes alguem; tagaini te to te wo torikumu illustrates mutual grappling hand to hand. The spacing teto teuo is retained in the canonical text.
Idem assigns the same grappling sense to the preceding Japanese example. It is a complete short physical continuation.
Torikurai means taking and eating greedily or without order. The crop shows no secure hyphen after sofre, so none is supplied before gamente.

runs.text: gamente, ou ſem ordem. Vide ſuprà,

lines.note: Gamente completes sofregamente; the cross-reference points back to toricui. The visible mark over final a in supra is a grave rather than a nasal tilde.
Completes the cross-reference Toricui, ǔ from the previous line. This is an abbreviated Japanese reference embedded in the Portuguese explanatory apparatus, not a new entry.
Toridashi means taking or bringing out. The scan separates Tirar fora, correcting OCR Tiranfora.

runs.text: Hum lugar botado mais pera fora

lines.note: The noun toridashi denotes a fortification projected farther outward. The spatial description continues with its relation to the main fortress below.

runs.text: das fortalezas como baluarte, ou forte contra

lines.note: Compares the outwork to a bulwark or fort against an enemy. Contra governs os inimigos on the following line.

runs.text: os inimigos. No Cami ſe diz,

lines.note: Completes the defensive purpose and gives dashi as the name used in Cami. Cami is the regional Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation; Daxi is its cited alternative.
Toride, with the historical form torizzuru, describes many people coming out. The following row specifies a rush or hurried crowd.
De tropel and com pressa explain emerging in a crowd or with haste. The printed ß-like type in preßa is retained as in the baseline.

runs.text: Fortaleza, ou forte, que eſtà perto da

lines.note: The noun toride is a fort near the principal fortress. The scan supports perto, correcting porto, and does not show a separate i after eſtà.
The smaller fort serves to guard the principal fortress better. Amilhor retains the close printed joining and historical milhor spelling.
Completes the watching or guarding purpose and supplies dashishiro as the Ximo regional name. The visible r gives Daxixiro rather than OCR Daxixito; this continuation is indented with its entry.

runs.text: Lugar, ou parte por onde ſe to-

lines.note: Toridokoro first denotes the place or part by which something is taken hold of. The divided to- begins tomar on the next line.

runs.text: ma, ou afferra dalgũa couſa. Item, permet.

lines.note: Completes tomar and pairs it with grasping something. Item, permet. introduces the figurative application to a person's qualities below.

runs.text: Partes, ou habilidade que ba em algum homem.

lines.note: The figurative sense is the qualities or ability present in a person. The scan prints ba with a closed bowl, unlike the h in habilidade and homem on the same row; the apparent anomaly is preserved rather than emended to expected ha.
Toridokoro nai hito describes a person with no redeeming or useful quality. The Portuguese negative clause continues over the next two rows.

runs.text: preſta pera nada, & que não tem nenhũa

lines.note: Says that the person is useful for nothing and possesses no good quality. The final vowel in não is o, correcting OCR nãa; nenhũa carries its visible abbreviation tilde.

Boa parte completes the description of having no good quality. The middle of boa is abraded, but the surviving word and complete phrase support the baseline reading; the row is an indented body continuation.
Toridori means in various ways or of varied kinds. The headword has r, not OCR f; Tori- starts the example on the next line.
Toridori ni moosu is speaking various things or expressing differing opinions. The initial F in Falar is clear, correcting Palar; di- begins dizer.
Completes dizer diversos pareceres, the explanation of expressing different opinions. This continues the preceding example rather than introducing a new headword.

runs.text: Acarne dagalinha, ou de outra aue

lines.note: Torihada first denotes the skin or flesh of a hen or other bird. The tight printed joins in Acarne and dagalinha are retained from the aligned baseline.

runs.text: de pois de depenada. ¶ Item, permet.

lines.note: Specifies the bird after plucking, then introduces the transferred sense applied to human skin. De pois is printed as two words.

runs.text: Carne, ou parte do corpo humano que eſtà aſpe-

lines.note: The transferred sense concerns human flesh or a body part made rough. Aſpe- begins aspera and connects to the effect of cold below.

runs.text: ra comfrio, como carne de paßaro depenado,

lines.note: Describes rough skin from cold, likened to a plucked bird. Comfrio preserves the printed close joining, while paßaro retains the baseline representation of the double-s type.

runs.text: que tem os pelos da carne, ou lugares a onde

lines.note: Explains the comparison through the skin hairs or sites where feathers were removed. A onde retains the printed spacing and introduces the next relative clause.
Finishes the gooseflesh comparison: the places from which feathers were pulled are raised or swollen. Inchados belongs to those sites in the preceding clause.
Torihadachi means developing gooseflesh. The headword reads Torifadachi, correcting Totifadachi; em continues into empolada below without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: polada, & aſpera comfrio naspartes dos ca-

lines.note: Completes empolada and describes the skin as raised and rough from cold around the hairs. Ca- begins cabelos on the next row.

runs.text: belos, como a das aues depenadas.

lines.note: Completes cabelos and repeats the comparison with plucked birds. This closes the verb entry corresponding to torifada above.
Torihanachi means throwing off, releasing, or detaching. The initial is T, not OCR F; the following row gives the written-register label.
Completes detaching from oneself or separating. The terminal S. is visibly upright and marks written usage, separate from the italic Portuguese gloss.
Torihanashi is the corresponding form used in ordinary speech. The next Item adds removal of an office or income; the headword begins with T.
Introduces removing someone's office or revenue. Yacu begins the Japanese illustration, with the alternative object chiguiǒuo on the next row.
Chigyoo wo torihanasu completes the example of taking away an income or fief. The final verb has long ſ before u, as printed.
Toriharai describes arranging or opening up a zashiki room by removing its partitions. The scan shows a capital T and a word gap after the Japanese room-name Zaxiqui, before tiran-.
Completes tirandolhe: removing the room's doors or partitions. This supplies the physical operation behind the preceding gloss.

runs.text: Torifayaxi, ſu, ita. l, torimochi, tçu.

lines.note: Torihayashi is paired with torimochi as an alternative. Fa- begins fazer in the Portuguese account of hospitality or favour.
Completes fazer agasalhado: showing hospitality, welcome, or favour. The printed noun form is retained without substituting a modern spelling.
Torihazushi first means letting go or allowing something to escape. The initial T corrects OCR F; fu- continues into fugir.

runs.text: gir a caſo como paßaro, &c. ¶ Item, Errar

lines.note: Completes accidentally letting a bird or similar creature escape. A new sense begins with errar, failing or making an error in taking something.

runs.text: no tomar. ¶ Item, Não alcançar o que ſe

lines.note: Completes failing to take or catch, then gives failure to obtain what one seeks. The relative clause continues with pretende below.
Completes the unattained-object sense; chigyoo wo tori hazuita illustrates failing to obtain revenue. The visible gui sequence corrects OCR Chigurǒuo, and the gap in tori fazzuita is retained.

runs.text: Não pode tomar, ou alcançar renda.

lines.note: The example means being unable to take or acquire an income. This confirms the preceding Japanese object chigyoo without modernizing its printed form.
Torihiroge means taking something and spreading it out. Eſ- starts estendella across the line division.

runs.text: tendella, ou eſtender ſem concerto, & ordẽ.

lines.note: Completes spreading out, with the added sense of spreading things without arrangement or order. The final ordẽ retains the printed abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Por as couſas a hũa par-

lines.note: Torihisome denotes putting things aside or away. The long ſ belongs to the Japanese stem, while par- begins parte in the gloss.

runs.text: te, ou em algũ lugar ſecreto, ou menos publico.

lines.note: Completes putting things to one side, in a secret or less public place. Publico has b, correcting OCR puhlico.
Torihishigi means breaking down, destroying, or crushing. The visible initial T corrects OCR F; the compact principal part da remains as printed.
Adds reducing something to small pieces, reinforcing the destructive sense of torifixigui. The cedilla in eſmiuçar is visible and retained.
Torihodoki means undoing, untying, or taking apart. The gloss continues with another near-synonym on the following row.

Adds the printed-looking desfazir as a synonym of undoing. The small vowel after z is abraded; the provisional i reading is retained with this caveat rather than silently normalizing to desfazer, and the spurious second final r is removed.
Torigai is identified simply as a kind of shellfish. The crop supports the headword's initial T, not OCR F; no species identification is supplied beyond the printed gloss.

runs.text: O tomar hũa couſa por outra. Vt,

lines.note: Torigaye denotes taking one thing in place of another. To- starts the example torigayeni suru on the next line.
Completes torigayeni suru, doing something by substitution or exchange. The short Japanese continuation is not a new independent entry.
Toriguchi, alternatively tori no hashi, denotes a smith's tongs. The scan shows the alternative marker l, omitted by OCR, and the whole Portuguese Tanaz de ferreiro is italic.

runs.text: Hũ portal q̃ eſta diante da ermida do Ca

lines.note: Torii is a gateway standing before the shrine of a kami. Ca continues in the displaced mi. at the far right of the next physical row; it is not an unfinished gloss or a separate entry.

Toriidashi means taking out. The separate far-right (mi. finishes Cami in the preceding torii definition; its physical placement on this row is preserved explicitly rather than inserted into the main text.

Toriide describes many people coming out or departing. Enlargement distinguishes two i types, without the j descender seen in Torijdaxi above; the subsequent NINJAL lexical checkpoint (263b18) also identifies Toriide. Partirſe corrects OCR parirſe.
The departure is hurried or disorderly. Enlargement shows a short s in desordem, correcting OCR detordem; this completes the Toriide gloss.
Toriinu denotes a dog used for hunting birds. The printed ij spelling joins the tori element to inu, without requiring an inserted space.
Toriire means taking something and putting it inside. The gloss continues with a second explanation of gathering or receiving within.
Completes the transitive action of putting or gathering inside. It contrasts with the following entry torijri, which describes entering.

Toriiri denotes entering or putting oneself within. Reinspection prompted by NINJAL 263b21 reveals two t types in itta, the first thin and worn, correcting OCR ita. The short terminal stroke after dentro is retained as printed although no word is divided there.

Zen no michi ni toriiru means entering the way of virtue; consonantal I in Ienno represents the z/j sound. Ca- continues as minho on the next page; the bottom minho catchword anticipates that continuation.
